source.title: Beyond Outliers: A Study of Optimizers Under Quantization
source.authors: Georgios Vlassis; Saleh Ashkboos; Alexandra Volkova; T. Hoefler; Dan Alistarh

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits and reports loss scaling laws in 4-bit quantization-aware training, an additional training regime, using OLMo2 models and optimizer-specific fits.
record.gate_note: The QAT test-loss results and fitted scaling-law coefficients bear on the claim. Full-precision losses are not included as rows because the claim versions tested here concern the QAT scaling analysis; downstream accuracies are not rows because they are not fitted or presented as predictable scaling relationships. The paper also reports PTQ results, but those address quantization robustness rather than the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits a saturating power law in N (Hoffmann form, reduced to iso-compute at D/N=20) to test loss for six optimizers. Each fit is joint over BF16 and 4-bit QuEST QAT OLMo2 runs from 50M to 1.5B, and the fitted curves and coefficients are reported (Fig. 5, Table 10). This is a new setting (quantized training, non-AdamW optimizers). The evidence is weak: the law is used mainly as a tool to compare optimizer parameter efficiency, no goodness-of-fit statistic is given, and the range is about 1.5 orders of magnitude.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors derive per-optimizer scaling laws fitted jointly to BF16 and 4-bit QAT losses, with a parameter-efficiency term ρ. They find Shampoo has the highest ρ4bit (0.879), followed by AdamW, and present this as supporting transfer of their QAT findings to larger scales. They do not test that transfer directly.
record.recipe_differences: The study adapts a scaling-law form cited from Hoffmann et al. to 4-bit QAT, adds optimizer-specific parameter efficiency, and fits an iso-compute version because the experiments use a fixed 20x token-to-parameter ratio.
record.method_sensitivity: Fitted coefficients and parameter efficiency vary with optimizer; the study uses a robust Huber fit and leave-one-out cross-validation for reported fit uncertainty.

fits_no_version.finding: Parameter efficiency of 4-bit QAT relative to BF16 differs by optimizer, from ρ4bit 0.739 (PSGD) to 0.879 (Shampoo).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effective-parameter penalty of low-precision training depends on the optimizer.

record.problems: The scaling fit uses a limited size range (50M to 1.5B) and a fixed token-to-parameter ratio; it does not independently estimate parameter, token, and compute scaling. The paper reports fit-parameter confidence intervals from leave-one-out cross-validation, but not a held-out small-to-large extrapolation test.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant QAT test-loss or fitted-law results were left out. Full-precision loss tables and zero-shot accuracy tables were not extracted as rows because they do not directly test the power-law loss versions recorded here.

untested.parts: Token and compute scaling are not separable: D/N is fixed at 20, so only the iso-compute N law is fitted. The range is ~50M–1.5B (about 1.5 orders), not several orders.
No small-to-large prediction test is reported. The authors only note that leaving out the largest model gave an unstable fit.
Not tested; D/N is fixed at 20.
Not tested; a single shape per size.
Quantized (W4A4 QAT) training is a further regime, but it is still text LM pretraining and is covered under V1. Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested.
Zero-shot accuracies are reported but not fitted or related to scale or loss.
Training schedule, data and fitting method are not varied. Bending away from a power law is not examined.

missing.what: BF16 full-precision test losses per optimizer and size. These are part of the data the scaling fits are run on but are not recorded as rows.
Including embedding parameters in N is stated to improve the fit (no numbers given). This is a parameter-counting choice affecting fit quality.

Leaving out the largest model in cross-validation gave an unstable fit, so the largest point was kept in all folds. This is qualitative evidence that the fits do not extrapolate robustly from smaller sizes.

record.verdict_notes: The scaling law is used chiefly as a comparison tool, and its fit quality is never quantified, so support for V1 is weak and limited to about 1.5 orders of magnitude. The record's V1 limits_scope label was removed because it described untested parts, which belong under untested. The α–E trade-off across optimizers (e.g., SOAP E=2.22 vs AdamW 1.40) suggests the coefficients are poorly identified from 5–6 points.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests parameter scaling for 4-bit QAT at a fixed 20x token-to-parameter ratio. It does not independently vary parameters, tokens, and compute, test conditions where the other quantities are not bottlenecks, or span several orders of magnitude.
The leave-one-out procedure is used to estimate fit-parameter confidence intervals; the paper does not report tests of whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
The study keeps the token-to-parameter ratio fixed and does not search for the loss-minimising parameter/token allocation as compute changes.
Only one architecture family is used; the study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer settings are tested.
Zero-shot accuracies are reported, but the study does not test whether downstream performance is predictably related to scale or pretraining loss.

The study reports optimizer-specific fits, but does not systematically vary parameter-count conventions, training schedules, data, or fitting methods to test their effects; it does not test curves bending away from a power law.

rows.measure: iso-compute test-loss scaling fit: A′, α, E, ρ4bit
rows.uncertainty: confidence intervals from leave-one-out cross-validation, reported as ± values
rows.note: The fitted law is L=A′/(N·ρ)^α+E; the fit uses the study's fixed token-to-parameter ratio.
rows.check: The fit is joint over BF16 (ρ=1) and W4A4 points per optimizer (Fig. 5; A.6 fits f(log N, log D, ρ b)), not QAT-only as the measure implies. No residuals or R² are reported, so 'observed' rests on the plotted curves only.
